system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

- SPA-N-009 | Riverlark facility | seller's draft: Post-completion release acceptable; ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding

- SPA-N-016 | Tax/IP open terms | seller's draft: Assume resolved / unlimited or general treatment

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel: Buyer-side review of the Seller's update and Disclosure Letter

## Bottom line

The package is not "fair and balanced." Taken together, the general disclosure, the knowledge exclusion, the limitations that apply to every claim and the 18-month limit mean the Buyer would have little effective warranty protection. Several known, quantifiable exposures are also left outside the price mechanics. The Seller's Disclosure Letter is more candid than its cover note and positions list, and we should use it against the Seller.

I have only the Seller's summary of its positions, not the full SPA draft or the DD-002 to DD-012 documents. Clause-level conclusions below need checking against those.

## Threshold point: "FINAL / settled at principal level"

I have no record on our side of any principal-level settlement, and the baseline I hold covers only price, debt-free/cash-free and NSW law. The "market" ranges are also the Seller's own assertion, so I wouldn't treat them as benchmarks. Please confirm with Wattlebridge's principals what, if anything, was agreed. Unless they confirm specific terms in writing, treat every position as open. Several positions are also internally inconsistent with the Seller's own Disclosure Letter, which weakens the "agreed bargain" claim.

## Priority 1: Value and closing-mechanics issues

**1. Riverlark (about AUD 3.2m): "release following Completion" is unacceptable.**
- On a debt-free/cash-free deal, the facility must be repaid at Completion from the price, under a payout letter, with discharge of security (PPSR and ASIC charges) delivered or held in escrow at Completion.
- Change-control clause 8.1 may also be triggered by the sale.
- The Disclosure Letter confirms the facility is unpaid and there is no discharge.
- Check whether Riverlark's security extends to the shares themselves, as this affects title (see item 8).

**2. DD-005 closing bonuses (AUD 420,000): not in the funds flow.**
- The bonuses are triggered by Completion, so the Company, which the Buyer will own, pays them. Calling them "a matter for the Seller" shifts the cost to us.
- Treat them as a Seller transaction cost or debt-like item deducted from the price.
- Include employer on-costs (superannuation, and NSW payroll tax where applicable). The Disclosure Letter expressly leaves these unaddressed. I'd estimate on-costs could add materially, perhaps in the order of 15-18%, but that needs payroll confirmation.

**3. Bluefen (about AUD 3.6m, about 30% of FY26 revenue).**
- The Seller says the consent is "addressed." Its own Disclosure Letter says no final consent or evidence of satisfied conditions exists.
- "Reasonable endeavours" and "satisfied on delivery of written consent" are inadequate. DD-002 clause 11.3 attaches conditions to consent.
- Make it a condition precedent to Completion, for the Buyer's sole benefit and waivable only by the Buyer. It should require unconditional consent, or consent on conditions acceptable to the Buyer, such as no repricing or termination rights.
- Require the Seller not to agree any concession to Bluefen without Buyer approval, and give the Buyer the right to participate in discussions.
- Add a termination right if consent isn't obtained by a long-stop date.

**4. Ironquay IP.**
- The existing indemnity covers only the AUD 180,000 SOW3 payment. DD-004 clause 7.3 makes the transfer of SOW3 Project Materials conditional on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. The real risk is whether the Company owns the code or materials, not the 180k.
- DD-010 is not independent verification of the amount, and there is no receipt or confirmatory assignment.
- Require, as a Completion deliverable, evidence of cleared payment and a written confirmatory assignment from Ironquay. This should include moral rights consents from individual contributors, which I'd also ask the Seller to confirm.
- Require an IP indemnity covering loss of title or use, remediation and re-development costs, sitting outside the general cap and basket.
- Check whether other statements of work contain the same payment-conditional transfer clause.

**5. DD-006 data incident (about 1,240 records).**
- "Preliminary operational matter, not expected to be material" is conclusory and unsupported. The Disclosure Letter says the Seller does not know whether the file was accessed, the scope, or whether notification is required.
- The Company appears large enough (revenue around AUD 12m, inferred from Bluefen being about 30% at AUD 3.6m) to be covered by the Privacy Act. If it is, the notifiable data breach regime has a 30-day assessment timeframe. The data room is dated 22 September, so that window may already have passed. Ask when the incident was discovered and whether an assessment and any notification were completed.
- Check whether the data belongs to customers such as Bluefen, whose contracts may carry their own breach-notification duties.
- Because the Seller disclosed this matter, a warranty claim is likely blocked. A specific indemnity is the only reliable protection. It should cover investigation, notification, regulatory and third-party claim costs, sit outside the cap, basket and de minimis, and run for several years.
- Require a forensic report and an updated status before signing, and Buyer control over the response between signing and Completion.

**6. Sandbar renewals (3 × AUD 110,000 = AUD 330,000).**
- Calling these "ordinary-course" is an assertion. The Disclosure Letter itself declines to say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary-course.
- Ask for the dates, term, termination rights, prepayment status, who approved them and whether Sandbar has any relationship with the Seller.
- Prepaid amounts, accrued amounts and commitments entered before Completion each affect the cash-free and debt-like analysis differently.
- Check whether the AUD 110,000 amount sits just under an internal approval threshold.
- Make sure the interim-period covenants require Buyer consent for new commitments.

**Identified-item total.** Riverlark, the bonuses and the open Ironquay fee come to about AUD 3.8m (about 16% of price), before on-costs, the Sandbar renewals and any incident cost. That is the amount currently sitting outside the price mechanics.

## Priority 2: Structural protections that would gut the warranties

**7. Disclosure and knowledge, working together.**
- Disclosing the entire data room plus public registers (Schedule 7, Disclosure Letter 1.1 and 1.2) means nothing is really warranted. Clause 8.3 then adds that the Buyer has no claim for anything "discoverable" from the data room, so the same material is excluded twice.
- Push for specific disclosure only, with fair disclosure meaning sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter. The Accounts should not be a general disclosure against the accounts warranties. Disclosure should not qualify the specific indemnities, the fundamental warranties or the conditions.
- Limit the knowledge clause to the actual knowledge of named Buyer deal-team individuals, with no constructive knowledge. Add an express statement that the Buyer's investigations do not limit its claims.
- Fix the disclosure cut-off date and require a bring-down. The data room snapshot is at 22 September and it is now 6 November. Insist on a full archived copy, and that later disclosure doesn't cure breaches or limit termination rights.

**8. Title and capacity warranties on the same cap and time limits.**
- This is a major departure from standard practice. Title and capacity warranties should be capped at the full purchase price. They should have a long limitation period, at least the 6-year NSW contract limitation period, and ideally no express time limit.
- A share register extract (DD-012) is the Seller's own document, and the Seller's letter expressly declines to say the Buyer has verified title.
- Do our own verification: ASIC extract, PPSR searches against both the Company and Harbourglass, the constitution (pre-emption and transfer restrictions), and any options, convertible instruments or employee equity.
- Check Harbourglass's own authority, including any fund or investor consents.
- Seek warranties of unencumbered title and a transfer deliverable at Completion.

**9. "Limitations apply to all Claims of any nature" (9.3, 12.8, 20.5).**
- As drafted, caps, time limits, the exclusive-remedy clause and non-reliance would apply to fraud, specific indemnities, tax, title and equitable relief.
- Reverse the default so limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims unless expressly stated.
- Carve out fraud and wilful concealment, the indemnities, fundamental and tax claims, and specific performance and injunctions.
- Non-reliance wording should not undermine misleading-conduct or fraud claims.

**10. Thresholds and caps.**
- The 20% cap (AUD 4.8m) isn't the main problem. Its scope is. Accept it only as a general warranty cap, with the carve-outs above.
- The AUD 250,000 basket (about 1.04% of price) is a deductible. Push for a tipping basket at a lower figure (opening ask nearer 0.5%), and a lower de minimis with aggregation of related claims, so a systemic data or IP issue isn't defeated claim by claim.
- Extend the general limit from 18 months to at least 24, so it covers two audit cycles.
- Tax and IP are not "settled under the general regime." Require a standalone tax indemnity and longer limits, tracking ATO amendment periods plus a buffer.

**11. Credit and security.**
- Harbourglass appears to be a holding vehicle that could distribute the proceeds. Seek a retention or escrow from the price sized to the specific indemnity exposures (Ironquay, the incident, Sandbar, bonus on-costs), or a parent or fund guarantee.
- If the Buyer considers warranty and indemnity insurance, known issues will be excluded, so the specific indemnities are needed regardless.

## Priority 3: Verify

- **Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009).** The Disclosure Letter carefully says the provisions "do not state" consent is required. It does not say consent is not required. I haven't seen the clauses. Check for change-of-control or deemed-assignment wording, and the timing and consequences of the lease notification. Add warranties, and consent as a condition if there is any doubt.

## Recommendations summary

| # | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Confirm with principals that nothing is actually "FINAL." Reject the market-norm framing. |
| 2 | Riverlark: payout letter and discharge at Completion, repaid from the price. |
| 3 | Bonuses (AUD 420k plus on-costs): deduct from the price as a Seller cost. |
| 4 | Bluefen: Buyer-only condition precedent requiring acceptable consent, with a long-stop termination right. |
| 5 | Ironquay: pre-Completion payment evidence, confirmatory assignment, and an IP indemnity outside the cap. |
| 6 | Data incident: forensic report and update now, specific uncapped indemnity, and Buyer control of the response. |
| 7 | Sandbar: documents and facts before agreeing treatment, plus interim-period covenants. |
| 8 | Disclosure: specific only, fairly disclosed, no data-room or register-wide disclosure, and a fixed cut-off with bring-down. |
| 9 | Knowledge: actual knowledge of named individuals only, with an express pro-Buyer reservation. |
| 10 | Title and capacity: price cap, long limit, and our own title verification, including PPSR and share-security checks. |
| 11 | Limitations: apply to general Warranty Claims only. Carve out fraud, indemnities, tax, fundamental claims and equitable relief. |
| 12 | Thresholds and time: tipping basket, lower de minimis with aggregation, at least 24 months, and a tax indemnity on ATO-linked periods. |
| 13 | Retention, escrow or guarantee to secure the indemnities. |
| 14 | Review DD-007 and DD-009 in full. |

On negotiation approach, I'd concede the 20% general cap only in exchange for the carve-outs, specific indemnities and retention. Those items matter more than the headline number. I can turn this into an issues list or a clause-by-clause mark-up once I have the full SPA draft and the DD documents.
=== END ADVICE ===
